transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yes, nice to meet you too. Thank you for seeing me. I, um... well, it's a bit of a long story, but I'll try to explain. I'm an auditor—I've been in accounting for years, got my bachelor's ages ago, and you'd think in my line of work that I'd have everything completely buttoned up. And I really try to. But what finally pushed me to make this appointment, what really made me realize I need to talk to someone, is that I keep starting these follow-up items at work and just... not finishing them. 

Like, after a massive audit wraps up, or even after these mentorship events I help run for the junior staff at the firm, there's always a list of wrap-up tasks. I will sit down at my desk with every intention of finishing them right then and there. I'll open the files, I'll start typing, I am fully engaged in getting it off my plate. But then, somehow, I find out days later that the task never actually got done. 

Someone will message me asking for a document, and I'll realize that the final email just sat in my drafts and I never hit send. Or a review note I swore I completed is just sitting there half-typed in the system. Or a compliance form never actually got submitted. And it is incredibly frustrating, and honestly so embarrassing, because I *know* I started it. I remember sitting there doing it! But the actual follow-through just sort of evaporates. I can't keep dropping the ball like this, especially not at my level, so... yeah, that's really why I'm here. It's just driving me crazy.
Did you have similar trouble finishing tasks when you were a child?

Oh, gosh, yes. Honestly, it goes all the way back to elementary school. It’s funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my mother about this the other day, and we were laughing—well, I was laughing, but also kind of wincing—about my old report cards. I mean, my parents kept everything, so I’ve actually seen them recently. Every single year, the teachers would write practically the same paragraph. They’d say I was bright, that I had so much potential, but then there would be this whole list of... well, issues. 

They’d say I was constantly losing my assignments, or I’d rush through things and make all these careless mistakes on the small details because I just wanted to be done with it. And I was always talking out of turn, interrupting people—which, frankly, I still have to stop myself from doing in meetings now. But the finishing tasks thing, absolutely. The teachers always noted that I needed constant reminders to actually finish my work. My mother still jokes about it to this day. She always says, "You could ace a test in five minutes, but you’d completely forget to hand in the big project that was literally sitting right there in your backpack." And it was true! I’d do the work, or at least start it, and then it would just live in my backpack until it was crumpled and three weeks late. So, yes, it’s definitely not a new problem, it’s just... it feels like it has higher stakes now, you know? When you're a kid, it's a zero on a diorama, but now it's a compliance form for a major client, and I just... I can't keep doing it.
Do you often find yourself worrying excessively about many different things, even when there isn’t a clear reason to?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I worry about things, sure, but it's usually very specific things. Like, if I know I have a massive audit coming up and the client is notorious for having their files in complete disarray, yes, I will stress about that. I'll lay in bed thinking about how long it's going to take to untangle their mess, and I'll worry about missing a deadline because of it. Or I'll worry about whether I remembered to send that email we were just talking about. But it's always tied to something real, something tangible that's actually happening in my life or at work. 

I don't just sit around agonizing over random things or having this vague sense of doom for no reason. My husband, actually, he's a bit of a worrier. He'll read the news and spend the whole evening stressing about the economy or something happening halfway across the world, and I just... I don't really operate like that. My brain is usually too busy bouncing between the ten things I'm supposed to be doing right now to invent things to worry about, if that makes sense. So, no, I don't think I have that kind of excessive, free-floating worry. It's more just the practical, immediate stress of trying to keep my head above water with all my tasks and making sure I don't drop the ball on something important.
Have you been losing interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

No, not really. I mean, I still love the things I love. It’s just... finding the time or the focus for them, you know? Like, I love gardening. Absolutely love it. My backyard is usually my sanctuary, and I have these raised beds that I built a few years ago—well, my husband helped, but I planned them all out—and I usually grow tomatoes, peppers, some herbs. And I still really enjoy the *idea* of it, and when I'm out there, I like it. But lately, it's more like I just can't get myself organized enough to actually go out and do the weeding or the pruning. 

I'll look out the window and think, "Oh, I really need to get out there, I want to get out there," but then I remember I have to put my gardening shoes on, and find my gloves, and where did I leave the pruning shears? Probably in the garage somewhere from last weekend when I meant to put them away but got distracted by the recycling bin... and by the time I think through all the steps, I just feel exhausted by the process and end up doing something else instead. But it's not that I don't *enjoy* gardening anymore. If someone handed me my gloves and shears and put me in front of the tomato plants, I'd be perfectly happy. It's the same with reading. I love a good mystery novel, but sitting down and actually focusing on a book when my brain feels like a pinball machine? It's tough. But the enjoyment is still there, definitely. I haven't lost that spark for the things I care about, it's just the execution that gets in the way.
